O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The review petitioner GRIDCO Limited is seeking review of common
judgment of this Tribunal dated 03.09.2025 rendered in appeal nos.254/2021
and 207/2022. Vide the said judgment, both these appeals were dismissed
and the orders dated 04.02.2020 and 04.04.2022 passed by the Central
Commission in petition nos.115/MP/2019 and 498/MP/2020 respectively
were upheld. Accordingly, GRIDCO Limited has been directed to pay to
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 2 of 22

GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd. the Fixed and Capacity Charges calculated in
accordance with the declared capacity basis as provided under the CERC
Tariff Regulations, 2014 for the disputed period 01.04.2015 to 31.03.2017.
It has been further held that GRIDCO Ltd. shall also be liable to pay
applicable Delayed Payment Surcharge in consonance with the terms of the
Power Purchase Agreement executed between the parties.
2. According to the review petitioner: -
(a) This Tribunal has erred in giving primacy to Regulation 30 of CERC
(Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2010 over Section 32
of the Electricity Act, 2003 without considering the submissions of
GRIDCO Ltd. in this regard;
(b) this Tribunal has failed to appreciate that definition of “Declared
Capacity” under Regulation 3(15) of CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014,
which refers to Grid Code (i.e. IEGC 2010) read with Regulation
6.4(a) of IEGC 2010 provides that the “Declared Capacity” is
governed as per the contract i.e. the Power Purchase Agreement
(PPA) and requisitions made by the buyers; and
(c) in terms of clause 2.2 of the PPA dated 04.01.2011 executed
between respondent no.1 GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd and
GRIDCO Ltd., GRIDCO’s contracted capacity is 25% of the power
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 3 of 22

sent out from the project of 1st respondent and accordingly, the Plant
Availability Factor i.e. monthly PAFM and the capacity charges have
to be computed on the basis of energy scheduled by GRIDCO
corresponding to 25% of total power sent out from the project of 1st
respondent.
3. We have heard Shri R K Mehta, learned counsel for the review
petitioner and Shri Vishrov Mukherjee, learned counsel for the 1st
respondent. We have also perused written submissions filed by the learned
counsels.
4. Learned counsel for the review petitioner argued that the view taken
by this Tribunal in the judgment dated 03.09.2025 that computation of PAFM
and payment of Fixed/Capacity Charges is governed only by provisions of
CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014 and not by contractual arrangement under
the PPA, is contrary to the Section 32 of the Electricity Act, 2003 as well as
CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014. It is further argued that even though the
submissions of GRIDCO in this regard have been noted in Paragraph nos.18
and 32 of the judgment under review, yet these have not been dealt with
anywhere in the judgment. It is submitted that the finding of the Tribunal that
GRIDCO is liable to make payment of Fixed Charges on the basis of
availability declarations by the 1st respondent GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 4 of 22

suffers from “error apparent” and is liable to be reviewed as the availability
declaration by GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd (GKEL) was contrary to the PPA
being more than 25%. Reliance, in this regard, is placed upon judgment
dated 18.11.2024 of this Tribunal in Review Petition No.3/2024, Uttar
Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited v. CERC and Ors. in which it has been
held that failure to note a statutory provision or failure to consider contentions
of a party are valid grounds for seeking review.
5. The learned counsel also referred to the judgments of the hon’ble
Supreme Court in S. Murali Sundaram v. Jothibai Kannan: 2023 SCC OnLine
SC 185 and Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) 6 SCC 224 to buttress his
submissions.
6. The review petition is vehemently resisted on behalf of the 1st
respondent GKEL. It is argued that the review petitioner GRIDCO has failed
to establish any “error apparent on the face of record” or “sufficient cause”
justifying the exercise of power of review. It is submitted that GRIDCO is
merely seeking re-adjudication/rehearing of the issues already adjudicated
by this Tribunal, under the guise of this review petition, which is
impermissible. It is further submitted that reference on behalf of GRIDCO to
Section 32 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and the submissions made in relation
thereto, are totally misplaced and devoid of any merit for the reason that
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 5 of 22

Section 32(2) of the Electricity Act, 2003 only provides for statutory functions
of SLDC (with regards to scheduling of power) and is in no manner
connected with computation of PAFM/Capacity Charges which is governed
in terms of Regulation 30 of CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014. In support of
his submissions, the learned counsel for GKEL relied upon the judgments of
the Supreme Court in Parsion Devi v. Sumitri Devi (1997) 8 SCC 715
(Para9), Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) 6 SCC 2241 (Para 56, 58),
State of W.B. v. Kamal Sengupta (2008) 8 SCC 612 (Para 22,23, 35) and
Kamlesh Verma v. Mayawati (2013) 8 SCC 320 (Paras 16-20.2).
Our Analysis: -
7. At the outset, we may note that Section 114 of CPC is the substantive
provision dealing with scope of review and is quoted below:
“114. Review. —Subject as aforesaid, any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has
been preferred.
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 6 of 22

allowed by this Code, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment
to the Court which passed the decree or made the
order, and the Court may make such order thereon
as it thinks fit.”
8. The grounds on which review of a judgment / order can be sought,
have been specified in Order XLVII of the CPC which are reproduced
hereinbelow: -
“1. Application for review of judgment. — (1) Any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed, but from which no appeal has been
preferred,
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 7 of 22

Small Causes, and who, from the discovery
of new and important matter or evidence which, after
the exercise of due diligence was not within his
knowledge or could not be produced by him at the
time when the decree was passed or order made,
or on account of some mistake or error apparent on
the face of the record or for any other sufficient
reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree
passed or order made against him, may apply
for a review of judgment to the Court which passed
the decree or made the order.
(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or
order may apply for a review of judgment
notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by
some other party except where the ground of such
appeal is common to the applicant and the
appellant, or when, being respondent, he can
present to the Appellate Court the case on which he
applied for the review.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 8 of 22

Explanation.—The fact that the decision on a
question of law on which the judgment of the Court
is based has been reversed or modified by the
subsequent decision of a superior Court in any other
case, shall not be a ground for the review of such
judgment.”
(Emphasis supplied)
9. A bare reading of these relevant legal provisions would make it clear
that an application for review of a judgment / order is maintainable upon (i)
discovery of a new and important matter or evidence which, after exercise of
due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the review applicant or could
not be produced by him when the judgment / order was passed; or (ii) on
account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of record; or (iii) for
any other sufficient reason.
10. The expression “error apparent on the face of record” used in Order
XLVII Rule 1 indicates an error which is self-evident and staring in the eye.
Any error or mistake which is not self-evident and has to be deducted from
a process of reasoning cannot be said to be an error apparent on the face of
record justifying exercise of power of review. Power of review can be
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 9 of 22

exercised only where a glaring omission or a patent mistake is found in the
order under review. We may also note that the power of review can be
exercised only for correction of a patent mistake but not to substitute a view
for the reason that a review petition cannot be permitted to be an appeal in
disguise.
11. In Chhajju Ram v. Neki Ram AIR 1922 PC 112, it was held that the
words “any other sufficient reason” appearing in Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC
must mean “a reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to those
specified in the rule”. This interpretation was approved by the Supreme Court
in later judgment in Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Most Rev. Mar
Poulose Athanasium 1955 1 SCR 520. In Kamlesh Verma v.
Mayawati & Ors. (2013) 8 SCC 320, Hon’ble Supreme Court has succinctly
summarized the principles for exercising review jurisdiction as under: -
“20. Thus, in view of the above, the following
grounds of review are maintainable as stipulated by
the stature:
20.1 When the review will be maintainable:
(i) Discovery of new and important matter or
evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence,
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 10 of 22

was not within knowledge of the petitioner or could
not be produced by him;
(ii) Mistake or error apparent on the face of the
record;
(iii) Any other sufficient reason.
The words “any other sufficient reason” have been
interpreted in Chhajju Ram v. Neki and approved by
this Court in Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v.
Most Rev. Mar Poulose Athanasius to mean “a
reason sufficient on grounds at least analogous to
those specified in the rule”. The same principles
have been reiterated in Union of India v. Sandur
manganese & Iron Ores Ltd.
20.2 When the review will not be maintainable:
(i) A repetition of old and overruled argument
is not enough to reopen concluded adjudications.
(ii) Minor mistakes of inconsequential import.
(iii) Review proceedings cannot be equated
with the original hearing of the case.
(iv) Review is not maintainable unless the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 11 of 22

material error, manifest on the face of the order,
undermines its soundness or results in miscarriage
of justice.
(v) A review is by no means an appeal in
disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard
and corrected but lies only for patent error.
(vi) The mere possibility of two views on the
subject cannot be a ground for review.
(vii) The error apparent on the face of the record
should not be an error which has to be fished out
and searched.
(viii) The appreciation of evidence on record is
fully within the domain of the appellate court, it
cannot be permitted to be advanced in the review
petition.
(ix) Review is not maintainable when the same
relief sought at the time of arguing the main matter
had been negatived.”
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 12 of 22

12. We also find advantageous to quote here following Paragraphs of the
judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in S. Madhusudhan Reddy v. V.
Narayana Reddy & Ors. (2022) SCC OnLine SC 1034:-
“31. As can be seen from the above exposition of
law, it has been consistently held by this Court in
several judicial pronouncements that the Court’s
jurisdiction of review, is not the same as that of an
appeal. A judgment can be open to review if there
is a mistake or an error apparent on the face of the
record, but an error that has to be detected by a
process of reasoning, cannot be described as an
error apparent on the face of the record for the
Court to exercise its powers of review under
Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC. In the guise of
exercising powers of review, the Court can correct a
mistake but not substitute the view taken earlier
merely because there is a possibility of taking two
views in a matter. A judgment may also be open to
review when any new or important matter of
evidence has emerged after passing of
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 13 of 22

thejudgment, subject to the condition that such
evidence was not within the knowledge of the party
seeking review or could not be produced by it when
the order was made despite undertaking an
exercise of due diligence. There is a clear
distinction between an erroneous decision as
against an error apparent on the face of the record.
An erroneous decision can be corrected by the
Superior Court, however an error apparent on the
face of the record can only be corrected by
exercising review jurisdiction. Yet another
circumstance referred to in Order XLVII Rule 1
for reviewing a judgment has been described as
“for any other sufficient reason”. The said phrase
has been explained to mean “a reason sufficient on
grounds, at least analogous to those specified in
the rule” (Refer: Chajju Ram v. Neki Ram and
Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Most Rev.
Mar Poulose Athanasius).”
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 14 of 22

13. In a recent judgment dated 08.09.2025 passed in Malleeswari v. K.
Suguna and Anr. SLP (C) No. 12787 of 2025 (2025 INSC 1080) Hon'ble
Supreme Court has again reiterated that court’s power to review its own
previous order is strictly limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of
the record and not to rehear or substitute a different view as if it were an
appeal. It has been held in the said judgment that the power of review is
different from appellate power and is subject to the following limitations to
maintain the finality of the judicial decisions:
“15.1 The review proceedings are not by way of an appeal and
have to be strictly confined to the scope and ambit of
Order 47 Rule 1 of CPC.
15.2 Review is not to be confused with appellate powers, which
may enable an appellate court to correct all manner of
errors committed by the subordinate court.
15.3 In exercise of the jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 of
CPC, it is not permissible for an erroneous decision to be
reheard and corrected. A review petition, it must be
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 15 of 22

remembered, has a limited purpose and cannot be
allowed to be an appeal in disguise.
15.4 The power of review can be exercised for the correction
of a mistake, but not to substitute a view. Such powers
can be exercised within the limits specified in the statute
governing the exercise of power.
15.5 The review court does not sit in appeal over its own order.
A rehearing of the matter is impermissible. It constitutes
an exception to the general rule that once a judgment is
signed or pronounced, it should not be altered. Hence, it
is invoked only to prevent a miscarriage of justice or to
correct grave and palpable errors.”
14. Further, after noticing the distinction between power of review and
appellate power, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has succinctly summed up the
grounds of review as under: -
“17.1 The ground of discovery of new and important matter or
evidence is a ground available if it is demonstrated that,
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 16 of 22

despite the exercise of due diligence, this evidence was
not within their knowledge or could not be produced by the
party at the time, the original decree or order was passed.
17.2 Mistake or error apparent on the face of the record may
be invoked if there is something more than a mere error,
and it must be the one which is manifest on the face of the
record. Such an error is a patent error and not a mere
wrong decision. An error which has to be established by a
long-drawn process of reasoning on points where there
may conceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be
an error apparent on the face of the record.
17.3 Lastly, the phrase 'for any other sufficient reason' means
a reason that is sufficient on grounds at least analogous
to those specified in the other two categories.”
15. We may also note that in the words of Justice Krishna Iyer (as his
Lordship then was), “a plea of review, unless the first judicial view is
manifestly distorted, is like asking for the Moon. A forensic defeat cannot be
avenged by an invitation to have a second look, hopeful of discovery of flows
and reversal of result. A review in the counsel’s mentation cannot repair the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 17 of 22

verdict once given. So, the law laid down must rest in peace.” (See
Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons (P) Ltd v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co.
Ltd. (2021) 9 SCC 657).
16. Bearing in mind these salutary legal principles governing the power of
a court to review its own decision, let’s now turn to the judgment under review
and the grounds of review raised in these petitions.
17. We may note that in the judgment under review, this Tribunal had
formulated following four issues for its consideration: -
Issue No. 1: Whether the methodology for computation of Plant
Availability Factor (Monthly) (PAFM) and payment of fixed/ capacity
charges for the period 01.04.2015 to 31.03.2017 ought to be
governed by the provisions of the CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014
or by the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)?
Issue No. 2: Whether CERC erred in relying upon the Minutes of
Meetings governing the parties' conduct during the relevant period?
Issue No. 3: Whether CERC incorrectly held that SLDC did not
compute the PAFM for the FY 2015-16 based on the original
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 18 of 22

availability declaration by GKEL vis-à-vis the subsequent revision
in the availability declaration by GKEL?
Issue No. 4: Whether GRIDCO can be made liable to pay fixed/
capacity charges (and Delayed Payment Surcharge) during
01.04.2015 to 31.03.2017?
18. Issue Nos.1&2 were taken together for adjudications. The discussion
of these two issues is found in Paragraph nos.32 to 69 of the judgment under
review.
19. In Paragraph no.54 we have referred to Regulation 30 of CERC Tariff
Regulations, 2014 and have explained how and why this regulation has an
overriding effect over inconsistent provision of contract between the
regulated entities. In Paragraph no.59, we have stated that the Tariff
Regulations, 2014 clearly require computation of PAFM and payment of
Fixed and Capacity Charges on the basis of declared availability in respect
of energy scheduled or withdrawal. In Paragraph no.60 we have noted that
the parties admit both (i) the regulatory requirement and (ii) that the prior
practice was inconsistent with the statutory norms. We have further held
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 19 of 22

that given the error in methodology which has been mutually recognized and
corrected w.e.f. 01.04.2017, equity demands that the same correction be
applied to the disputed period unless compelling contractual or legal
constraints dictate otherwise.
20. Even though, we have not specifically referred to Section 32 of the
Electricity Act, 2003, yet it is axiomatic that this legal provision is primarily
concerned with the statutory functions of State Load Dispatch Centre, as the
heading of the section denotes. It is in no manner connected with the
computation of PAFM/Capacity Charges which is governed by Regulation 30
of CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014. We have also based our findings on these
two issues on the said Regulation 30 of CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014,
which are in no way contrary to or inconsistent with Section 32 of the
Electricity Act, 2003.
21. The discussion on Issue No.4, which relates to liability of GRIDCO to
pay fixed/capacity charges, (and delayed payment surcharge) spans from
Paragraph no.79 to 98 of the judgment under review. The contention on
behalf of GRIDCO that it cannot be made liable to pay capacity charges for
the power it did not avail, have been discussed and dealt with in Paragraph
no.87 to 90 and 96 to 98 of the judgment under review. Further, the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 20 of 22

contention on behalf of the review petitioner that it had not raised revised bill
on the basis of PAFM % certified by SLDC as mandated under Article 7.1.1
of the PPA have been considered and rejected in Paragraph nos.92 to 94 of
the judgment under review.
22. In nutshell, we may note that upon consideration of all the relevant
statutory provisions as well as regulations, this Tribunal has, in the judgment
under review, come to a particular finding on the issue under consideration
which cannot be altered in the review proceedings. A well-reasoned and well
considered judgment, even though erroneous, does not fall within the scope
and ambit of review. There is a clear distinction between a judgment
suffering from error apparent on the face of record and an erroneous
judgment. Review petition is maintainable only in the former case whereas
in the latter case, the remedy available to the aggrieved party is to assail the
order/judgment by way of appeal in the higher forum/court.
23. By way of the instant review petition, the petitioner is actually seeking
a relook of the judgment under review in the hope to discover any flaw or
fault in the same, which is not permissible in law. The review petition
manifestly appears to be appeal in disguise and thus, does not fall within the
scope and ambit of Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.31 of 2025 Page 21 of 22

24. Hence, we are of the considered opinion that the petitioner has failed
to make out any mistake or error apparent on the face of record in the
judgment under review dated 03.09.2025 and has failed to bring the case
within the parameters laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various
decisions referred to hereinabove. The review petition is sans any merit and
is accordingly dismissed.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 03rd day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The review petitioner is seeking review of judgment of this Tribunal
dated 26.05.2025 passed in appeal no.130 of 2019 whereby the said appeal
was partly allowed. The grievance of the petitioner is with regards to the
findings returned by this Tribunal on Issue No.(ii) in the said judgment which
was with regards to “Consideration of the actual interest on working capital
as ‘NIL’ in True-up for FY 2016-17”. The findings of the Commission on this
issue have been affirmed in the judgment under review.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 2 of 16

2. Upon consideration of the rival submissions of the parties in the light
of the applicable Regulation 31.6 of MYT Regulations, 2015, this Tribunal
has held that in view of the proviso to Regulation 31.6, contribution/impact of
Delayed Payment Surcharge (DPS) to the actual interest on working capital
ought to be deducted from the actual interest on working capital while
computing the efficiency gain or efficiency loss.
3. We have heard Mr. P. Chidambaram and Mr. M G Ramachandran,
learned senior counsels appearing on behalf of the review petitioner, Ms.
Pratiti Rungta, learned counsel for the 1st respondent and Mr. S.K.
Parmeshwar, learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the 2nd
respondent.
4. Learned senior counsels appearing for the review petitioner submitted
that normative interest on working capital cannot be a subject matter of
adjustment under the proviso to Regulation 31.6 and if the actual interest on
working capital is less than normative interest on working capital, there would
be efficiency gain on the part of the generator, the generator actually having
incurred less interest on working capital. If, on the other hand, actual interest
on working capital is more than the normative, there would be efficiency loss
on the part of the generator. It is submitted that the main part of Regulation
31.6 targets such efficiency gain/loss, as the case may be, which is provided
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 3 of 16

for sharing and not any part of normative interest on working capital. This
was sought to be explained by way of following illustration: -
“To illustrate: If the normative Interest on working capital is
Rs. 100, the actual interest on working capital incurred can
be higher say Rs. 121 or lower say Rs. 79. In such cases:
(i) The variance of Rs. 21 in Rs. 121 is the efficiency loss;
the Generator will not be allowed the entire Rs. 21 from
MSEDCL but only restricted to 1/3rd as per Regulation
11 and the balance 2/3rd to be assumed by the
Generator. This 1/3rd of Rs. 21 will be in addition to the
Normative Interest on Working Capital; and
(ii) The variance of Rs. 21 in Rs. 79 is the efficiency gain;
the Generator will be allowed to retain 1/3rd of Rs. 21,
namely, Rs. 7 as per Regulation 11 in addition to the
Normative Interest on Working Capital and the balance
2/3rd, namely, Rs. 14 will be accounted for the benefit of
MSEDCL.
(iii) In the actual interest on working capital computation,
such variance of Rs. 21, as per the main part of
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 4 of 16

Regulation 31.6 is, however subject to deduction of
contribution of delay in receipt of payment to actual
interest on working capital as per the proviso. The entire
sharing to the benefit of the Review Petitioner, i.e., Rs. 7
may be wiped out by reason of the contribution of the
delayed payment surcharge accrued but the adjustment
cannot extend to the Normative Interest on Working
Capital.
As per Regulation 31.6 the extent of sharing of Efficiency
gain or Efficiency loss, as the case may be, will be
restricted to Rs. 7. Whereas the State Commission's
Order Impugned in the Appeal adjusts the entire
Normative Interest on working capital of Rs. 100 in
addition to Rs. 7 qua the delayed payment surcharge as
efficiency loss adjustment, which is not as per Paras 22
and 23 of the decision of this Hon'ble Tribunal on the
plain reading of Regulation 31.6. For example, if the
Normative interest on working capital as also the accrual
interest on working capital is exactly same namely Rs
484.41 crores then Regulation 31.6 will have no have
any application, whereas if the difference is say only Rs.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 5 of 16

10 then Regulation 31.6 will make the working capital
requirement to be NIL as per State Commission. This
would lead to anomalous and absurd result that the
Review Petitioner has no working capital requirement.
(iv) It is respectfully submitted that this Hon'ble Tribunal
construing Regulation 31.6 proviso on the reasoning
given in Paras 22 and 23 [Pages 45-47] could not have
intended to deal with normative interest on working
capital also (Rs. 100 in the above example) which would
be going beyond the zone of consideration of 'variance'.
The effect of para 24 of the Order dated 26.05.2025
[Page 47] upholding the decision of the State
Commission will lead to the above.
(v) In the present case, admittedly the Normative Interest on
Working Capital is Rs. 484.41 crores [Para 5.21.8, Page
555-556], and the actual interest on working capital is Rs.
602.78 Crores and the difference of Rs. 118.37 Crores is
the Zone of consideration and not the entire Rs. 484.41
Crores or any part of Rs. 484.41 Crores.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 6 of 16

(vi) It is settled law that the proviso cannot exceed the scope
of the main provision and it only qualifies the
circumstances dealt in the main provision.”
5. It is further argued that the term “receipt” in Regulation 31.6 refers to
the loan from the bankers of the generating company and then it would relate
to the delay in the payment of interest on working capital loan by the
generating company. It is argued that there is no implication or impact of
DPS which the 2nd respondent MSEDCL is obligated to pay for delay in the
payment of monthly bills. The submission is that DPS is for the period after
the due date for payment of monthly/supplementary bills and is dealt with in
Regulation 36 whereas Regulation 31.6 including proviso, deals with an
independent aspect of sharing of efficiency gain or efficiency loss or variance
between normative or actual which is provided in Regulation 11.
6. The review petition is vehemently opposed on behalf of the
respondents on the ground that none of the conditions as stipulated in Order
XLVII Rule 1 of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 are met in the review petition.
7. It is argued that no mistake or error apparent on the face of record in
the judgment under review has been demonstrated by the review petitioner
and no sufficient reason, that would justify the review of the judgment of this
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 7 of 16

Tribunal, has been made out. It is pointed out that the grounds in the present
review petition are verbatim repetition of what was argued during the hearing
of the appeal and rejected in the judgment under review, and therefore, the
instant review petition, being an appeal in disguise, cannot be entertained.
Our Analysis:
8. At the outset, we may note that Section 114 of CPC is the substantive
provision dealing with scope of review and is quoted below:
“114. Review. —Subject as aforesaid, any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal has
been preferred.
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed by this Code, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, may apply for a review of judgment
to the Court which passed the decree or made the
order, and the Court may make such order thereon
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 8 of 16

as it thinks fit.”
9. The grounds on which review of a judgment / order can be sought,
have been specified in Order XLVII of the CPC which are reproduced
hereinbelow: -
“1. Application for review of judgment. — (1) Any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed, but from which no appeal has been
preferred,
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, and who, from the discovery
of new and important matter or evidence which, after
the exercise of due diligence was not within his
knowledge or could not be produced by him at the
time when the decree was passed or order made,
or on account of some mistake or error apparent on
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 9 of 16

the face of the record or for any other sufficient
reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree
passed or order made against him, may apply
for a review of judgment to the Court which passed
the decree or made the order.
(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or
order may apply for a review of judgment
notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by
some other party except where the ground of such
appeal is common to the applicant and the
appellant, or when, being respondent, he can
present to the Appellate Court the case on which he
applied for the review.
Explanation.—The fact that the decision on a
question of law on which the judgment of the Court
is based has been reversed or modified by the
subsequent decision of a superior Court in any other
case, shall not be a ground for the review of such
judgment.”
(Emphasis supplied)
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 10 of 16

10. A bare reading of these relevant legal provisions would make it clear
that an application for review of a judgment / order is maintainable upon (i)
discovery of a new and important matter or evidence which, after exercise of
due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the review applicant or could
not be produced by him when the judgment / order was passed; or (ii) on
account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of record; or (iii) for
any other sufficient reason.
11. The expression “error apparent on the face of record” used in Order
XLVII Rule 1 indicates an error which is self-evident and staring in the eye.
Any error or mistake which is not self-evident and has to be deducted from
a process of reasoning cannot be said to be an error apparent on the face of
record justifying exercise of power of review. Power of review can be
exercised only where a glaring omission or a patent mistake is found in the
order under review. We may also note that the power of review can be
exercised only for correction of a patent mistake but not to substitute a view
for the reason that a review petition cannot be permitted to be an appeal in
disguise.
12. In a recent judgment dated 08.09.2025 passed in Malleeswari v. K.
Suguna and Anr. SLP (C) No. 12787 of 2025 (2025 INSC 1080) Hon'ble
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 11 of 16

Supreme Court has reiterated that court’s power to review its own previous
order is strictly limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of the record
and not to rehear or substitute a different view as if it were an appeal. It has
been held in the said judgment that the power of review is different from
appellate power and is subject to the following limitations to maintain the
finality of the judicial decisions:
“15.1 The review proceedings are not by way of an appeal and
have to be strictly confined to the scope and ambit of
Order 47 Rule 1 of CPC.
15.2 Review is not to be confused with appellate powers, which
may enable an appellate court to correct all manner of
errors committed by the subordinate court.
15.3 In exercise of the jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 of
CPC, it is not permissible for an erroneous decision to be
reheard and corrected. A review petition, it must be
remembered, has a limited purpose and cannot be
allowed to be an appeal in disguise.
15.4 The power of review can be exercised for the correction
of a mistake, but not to substitute a view. Such powers
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 12 of 16

can be exercised within the limits specified in the statute
governing the exercise of power.
15.5 The review court does not sit in appeal over its own order.
A rehearing of the matter is impermissible. It constitutes
an exception to the general rule that once a judgment is
signed or pronounced, it should not be altered. Hence, it
is invoked only to prevent a miscarriage of justice or to
correct grave and palpable errors.”
13. Further, after noticing the distinction between power of review and
appellate power, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has succinctly summed up the
grounds of review as under: -
“17.1 The ground of discovery of new and important matter or
evidence is a ground available if it is demonstrated that,
despite the exercise of due diligence, this evidence was
not within their knowledge or could not be produced by the
party at the time, the original decree or order was passed.
17.2 Mistake or error apparent on the face of the record may
be invoked if there is something more than a mere error,
and it must be the one which is manifest on the face of the
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 13 of 16

record. Such an error is a patent error and not a mere
wrong decision. An error which has to be established by a
long-drawn process of reasoning on points where there
may conceivably be two opinions can hardly be said to be
an error apparent on the face of the record.
17.3 Lastly, the phrase 'for any other sufficient reason' means
a reason that is sufficient on grounds at least analogous
to those specified in the other two categories.”
14. We may also note that in the words of Justice Krishna Iyer (as his
Lordship then was), “a plea of review, unless the first judicial view is
manifestly distorted, is like asking for the Moon. A forensic defeat cannot be
avenged by an invitation to have a second look, hopeful of discovery of flows
and reversal of result. A review in the counsel’s mentation cannot repair the
verdict once given. So, the law laid down must rest in peace.” (See
Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons (P) Ltd v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co.
Ltd. (2021) 9 SCC 657).
15. We now turn to the instant review petition while keeping in mind the
above noted salutary legal principles enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme
Court governing the power of a court to review its own decision.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 14 of 16

16. A perusal of the judgment under review would reveal that there has
been elaborate discussion on the issue which is agitated in the review
petition by the petitioner. All the arguments advanced in this regard on behalf
of the review petitioner during the course of hearing of appeal have been
noted and dealt with. The discussion on this issue alone spans over seven
pages of the judgment i.e. from Paragraph nos.17 to 24. We have noted
Regulation 31.6 of MYT Regulations, 2015 in Paragraph no.21 and have
interpreted it in Paragraph no.22. The submissions in this regard made on
behalf of the review petitioner have been noted and discussed in Paragraph
no.23. It is not the case of the review petitioner that any argument advanced
on its behalf has not been noted and considered in the judgment. Thus, it is
evident that this Tribunal, in the judgment under review, has come to a
particular finding on the issue under consideration upon consideration of the
relevant regulations as well as the rival submissions of the learned counsels
for the parties, which cannot be altered in the review proceedings. Well-
reasoned and well considered judgment, even though erroneous, does not
fall within the scope and ambit of review. There is a clear distinction between
a judgment suffering from error apparent on the fact of record and erroneous
judgment. Review petition is maintainable only in the former case whereas
in the latter case, the remedy available to the aggrieved party is to assail the
order/judgment by way of appeal in the higher forum/court.
____________________________________________________________________________________
RP No.20 of 2025 Page 15 of 16

17. By way of the instant review petition, the petitioner is actually seeking
a relook of the judgment under review in the hope to discover any flaw or
fault in the same, which is not permissible in law. The review petition
manifestly appears to be appeal in disguise and thus, does not fall within the
scope and ambit of Order XLVII Rule 1 of the CPC.
18. Hence, we are of the considered opinion that the petitioner has failed
to make out any mistake or error apparent on the face of record in the
judgment under review dated 26.05.2025 and has failed to bring the case
within the parameters laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in various
decisions referred to hereinabove. The review petition is sans any merit and
is accordingly dismissed.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 03rd day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)

O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. By way of this application, the appellants have sought condonation
of delay of 368 days delay in filing the instant appeal.
2. Appellant No.1 is a public limited company and the successor in
interest of erstwhile ACME Solar Holdings Limited. Appellant no.2 is a
special purpose vehicle incorporated by appellant no.1 for developing and
commissioning 300MW grid connected solar photovoltaic power project.
3. In pursuance to Request for Selection (RfS) dated 06.05.2021, the
appellant no.1 submitted its bid and was declared successful for
development of the said solar power project.
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 2 of 22

4. It appears that there was delay on the part of the appellants in
completion and commissioning of the power project within the stipulated
time. Accordingly, the appellants approached the Commission with
petition no.326/MP/2024 seeking extension of time period for
commissioning of the solar power project by three months with further
direction to 2nd respondent CTUIL not to take any coercive action with
regard to the connectivity granted to the appellants for the power project
on 10.05.2022. The petition has been disposed of by the Commission
vide order dated 25.11.2024 which has been impugned in this appeal. The
Commission, while allowing extension of time for the completion of power
project till 21.04.2025 has directed the appellant to pay compensation to
the 2nd respondent CTUIL as condition for retention of the connectivity
granted at Bikaner-II transmission line.
5. Being aggrieved by the direction to pay compensation to CTUIL for
retaining the connectivity, the appellants have approached this Tribunal
by way of the instant appeal. As already noted hereinabove, there is delay
of 368 days in filing the appeal.
6. Before adverting to the rival contentions and submissions of the
parties on the aspect of condonation of delay in filing the appeal, we find
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 3 of 22

it necessary to note following events which are very material for a decision
on the application at hand.
7. Subsequent to the passing of the impugned order by the
Commission on 25.11.2024, the appellant filed review petition bearing
no.3/RP/2025 on 01.01.2025 seeking review of the impugned order.
However, the review petition was withdrawn by the appellants on
20.02.2025. Thereafter, the appellants approached the Commission
again by way of petition no.452/MP/2025 seeking extension of further 65
days i.e. till 25.06.2025 for commissioning of the power project. However,
during the pendency of the said petition, CTUIL vide its letter dated
23.04.2025, revoked the connectivity granted to the appellants. When this
fact was brought to the notice of the Commission, the Commission vide
record of proceedings dated 24.04.2025 directed CTUIL to keep
revocation in abeyance and permitted the appellants to proceed with the
commissioning activities. Ultimately, the project was commissioned by
the appellants on 25.06.2025. The said interim order dated 24.04.2025
remained in operation till the issuance of final order dated 12.12.2025 in
the said petition no.452 of 2025.
8. It appears that the temporary connectivity granted to the appellants
was not being fully operationalized and thus, the appellants filed a writ
petition bearing no.13641 of 2025 before the Hon’ble Delhi High Court on
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 4 of 22

02.09.2025 seeking issuance of appropriate directions to the relevant
government authorities for the timely operationalization of the
connectivity/GNA granted to the appellants’ power project. It is relevant
to note here that in the status report dated 22.09.2025 filed by CTUIL and
PowerGrid Narela Transmission Limited (PNTL) in the said writ petition it
was acknowledged that Khetri-Narela line was likely to be commissioned
only by December, 2025.
9. PNTL declared commercial operation of Khetri-Narela Transmission
Line on 10.12.2025. Accordingly, connectivity for all the projects
connected to Bikaner-II except the appellants was made effective by
CTUIL on the said dated i.e. 10.12.2025.
10. Thereafter, in pursuance to the final order passed by the
Commission in petition no.452 of 2025 on 12.12.2025, CTUIL restored the
connectivity of the appellants at Bikaner-II and made the GNA for
appellants’ 300MW power project at Bikaner-II effective from 14.12.2025.
Thus, the appellants were allowed to evacuate the entire 300MW power
from the project.
11. Thereafter, the appellants filed the instant appeal on 12.01.2026.
12. We have heard Ms. Suparna Srivastava, learned counsel for the
appellant/applicant and Ms. Poorva Saigal, learned counsel for the 2nd
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 5 of 22

respondent CTUIL. We have also perused the pleadings of the parties on
the aspect of condonation of delay in filing the appeal.
13. Learned counsel for the appellants would argue that the issues
arising from the impugned order were linked with the pending proceedings
before the Commission concerning the commissioning of the project,
revocation and restoration of connectivity as well as operationalization of
the associated transmission system and the legal position became crystal
clear only on passing of final order dated 12.12.2025 by the Commission
in petition no.452 of 2025. It is submitted that the appellants found it
appropriate to wait for the crystallization of the issues and the final
resolution of interconnected proceedings before approaching this Tribunal
by way of the instant appeal, in order to avoid multiplicity of proceedings
and inconsistent adjudication.
14. It is argued that the delay in filing the appeal was occasioned due to
circumstances wholly beyond the control of the appellants which included
the delay in commissioning of associated ISTS, revocation of connectivity
by CTUIL during the pendency of the proceedings of petition no.452 of
2025, restricted evacuation granted to the appellants under temporary
GNA and the imminent risk of shutdown of the power project. It is argued
that during this period the appellants were constrained to focus on
safeguarding the commissioning of the project in order to ensure
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 6 of 22

uninterrupted supply of entire 300MW power from the project and
utilization of the connectivity to avoid irreparable financial and operational
harm. It is submitted that delay in filing the appeal was entirely attributable
to the need for due diligence and careful preparation, rather than lack of
bonafide intention or diligence on the part of the appellants. The learned
counsel cited the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Maniben
Devraj Shah v. Municipal Corporation of Brihan Mumbai, (2012) 5 SCC
157 and Isha Bhattacharjee v. Managing Committee of Raghunathpur
Nafar Academy (2013) 12 SCC 649 in support of her submissions.
15. Per contra, the learned counsel for the 2nd respondent CTUIL would
argue that pendency of parallel unconnected proceedings with separate
cause of action/relief before other fora cannot be made a ground to
suspend or extend the period of limitation for filing of the appeal before
this Tribunal against the impugned order dated 25.11.2024. She
submitted that the conduct of the appellants reflects not only lack of due
diligence but also deliberate tactics to prolong litigation and admitting such
a belated appeal would not only defeat the scheme of limitation but would
also unsettle regulatory certainty and would cause grave prejudice to
CTUIL as well as other connectivity grantees.
16. Citing the judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court in P.K.
Ramachandran v. State of Kerala (1997) 7 SCC 556 and Chhattisgarh
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 7 of 22

SEB v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (2010) 5 SCC 23, the
learned counsel submitted that special limitation period prescribed under
Section 111 and 125 of the Electricity Act, 2003 are to be strictly adhered
to in order to preserve the legislative intent of expeditious adjudication by
an expert body. According to the learned counsel, the appellants have
failed to demonstrate any legally sustainable explanation constituting
“sufficient cause” for not approaching this Tribunal within the prescribed
period of limitation. Referring to another recent judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ramkumar Choudhary,
2024 SCC OnLine SC 3612, the learned counsel would submit that a
party seeking condonation of delay must explain the failure to file the
appeal within the statutory period of limitation itself and the subsequent
development cannot justify the delay.
17. The learned counsel further argued that the conduct of the
appellants clearly demonstrates that they consciously chose to pursue
unrelated proceedings before other foras rather than invoking the
statutory appellate jurisdiction of this Tribunal within the prescribed period
of limitation. According to her, the sequence of events that took place
subsequent to the passing of impugned order by the Commission reveals
a clear pattern on the part of the appellants to indulge in forum shopping.
She submitted that the appellants have failed to demonstrate any
circumstances which prevented them from approaching this Tribunal
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 8 of 22

within the statutory period of 45 days prescribed under Section 111 of the
Electricity Act, 2003 and buttressed her submissions by relying upon
another judgment of the Supreme Court in Shivamma (Dead) by LRs v.
Karnataka Housing Board & Ors., 2025 INSC 1104. She also relied upon
Basawaraj and Anr. v. Special Land Acquisition Officer (2013) 14 SCC 81
to argue that discretion to condone delay must be exercised judiciously
and not on sympathetic grounds.
18. Thus, on the basis of these submissions, the learned counsel sought
dismissal of the application.
19. We have considered the rival submissions of the learned counsels
and have gone through the averments made by the appellants in the
application and by the 2nd respondent in the reply filed to the application.
We have also perused the judgments cited at bar by the learned counsels.
20. The judgment of the Apex Court in Shivamma case (supra) is relied
upon by both the learned counsels. The learned counsel for the 2nd
respondent CTUIL has drawn our attention to Paragraph No.23 and 40 of
the judgment which are extracted hereinbelow: -
“23. In Ramkumar Choudhary (supra), this very Bench
had the occasion to examine the meaning of the expression
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 9 of 22

“within such period” used in Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Placing reliance on the decisions of this Court in Ajit Singh
Thakur (supra) and Basawaraj (supra), it was held that for
the purpose of Section 5, the party seeking condonation of
delay has to explain why it was unable to institute the
proceedings within the prescribed period of limitation.
Events that occurred after the expiry of the period of
limitation till the date of actual filing of the appeal or
application, as the case may be, would be of no
consequence insofar as condonation is concerned, if it is
unable to explain what came in the way of the party that it
was unable to file it. It reiterated that no event or
circumstance arising after the expiry of limitation can
constitute such sufficient cause, where the party allowed the
limitation to expiry unless it can trace such failure in allowing
the limitation to expire to a cause arising within the period of
limitation. The relevant observations read as under:-
…..
40. As such, under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, for
the purpose of seeking condonation of delay in filing of an
appeal or application, as the case may be, beyond the
stipulated period of limitation, the delay in the filing has to be
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 10 of 22

explained by demonstrating the existence of a “sufficient
cause” that resulted in such delay for both the prescribed
period of limitation as-well as the period after the expiry of
limitation, up to actual date of filing of such appeal or
application, as the case may be, or to put it simply,
explanation has to be given for the entire duration from the
date when the clock of limitation began to tick, up until the
date of actual filing, for seeking condonation of delay by
recourse to Section 5 of the Limitation Act.”
21. Thus, in view of the legal principle enunciated in the above referred
Paragraphs of the judgment, while citing with approval the earlier
judgments in Ramkumar Choudhary’s case (supra) and Basawaraj
(supra), the delay in filing has to be explained by demonstrating existence
of “sufficient cause” that prevented the appellants from filing the appeal
both within the prescribed period of limitation as well as the period after
the expiry of limitation period up to the actual date of filing. However,
Paragraphs 136 and 137 of the judgment are also material, which have
been referred to by learned counsel for the appellants, and are extracted
hereinbelow: -
“136 When technical considerations of limitation conflict
with the imperative of substantial justice, the latter should
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 11 of 22

ordinarily prevail. Rules of limitation are not designed to
destroy the rights of parties but to prevent inordinate delay
in seeking remedies. Thus, the interpretation of “sufficient
cause” must be liberal and purposive, aimed at advancing
the cause of justice rather than defeating it. This is why the
courts, while construing applications for condonation of
delay, emphasize the bona fides of the applicant over the
sheer arithmetical length of the delay.
137. Where strict adherence to these rules results in
injustice, the Court is dutybound to apply a liberal
interpretation of “sufficient cause” so as to balance technical
requirements with the demands of justice. A litigant does not
stand to benefit by lodging an appeal late, and therefore, a
pragmatic and justice-oriented approach must inform the
judicial discretion under Section 5. This decision continues
to be the most frequently cited authority for the proposition
that the judiciary should incline towards justice rather than
technicality. Therefore, when courts interpret “sufficient
cause,” they are expected to exercise discretion in a manner
that fosters justice, fairness, and equity, keeping in mind the
realities of litigation.”
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 12 of 22

22. Thus, while deciding an application for condonation of delay, the
courts are duty bound to give a liberal interpretation to the term “sufficient
cause” in order to balance the technical requirements with the demands
of justice and are expected to exercise discretion in a manner that fosters
justice, fairness and equity, while keeping in mind realities of litigation.
23. In Maniben’s case also, the Supreme Court has advocated liberal
and justice oriented approach in exercise of power under Section 5 of the
Limitation Act and other similar statutes but has cautioned that courts
cannot be oblivious of the fact that a successful litigant has acquired
certain rights on the basis of the judgment under challenge and a lot of
time has been consumed at various stages of litigation apart from the
costs. The judgment laid down the principle that if the courts find that
there has been no negligence on the part of the appellant and the cause
shown for delay does not lack bonafides, then it may condone the delay
but on the other hand, if the explanation given by the applicant is found to
be concocted or he has been thoroughly negligent in prosecuting his case,
it would be a legitimate exercise of discretion not to condone the delay.
24. In Isha Bhattacharjee case, the Apex Court has enunciated
following principles to be kept in mind while deciding an application for
condonation of delay: -
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 13 of 22

“i) There should be a liberal, pragmatic, justice-oriented,
non-pedantic approach while dealing with an application for
condonation of delay, for the courts are not supposed to
legalise injustice but are obliged to remove injustice.
ii) The terms sufficient cause should be understood in their
proper spirit, philosophy and purpose regard being had to
the fact that these terms are basically elastic and are to be
applied in proper perspective to the obtaining fact-situation.
iii) Substantial justice being paramount and pivotal the
technical considerations should not be given undue and
uncalled for emphasis.
iv) No presumption can be attached to deliberate causation
of delay but, gross negligence on the part of the counsel or
litigant is to be taken note of.
v) Lack of bona fides imputable to a party seeking
condonation of delay is a significant and relevant fact.
vi) It is to be kept in mind that adherence to strict proof should
not affect public justice and cause public mischief because
the courts are required to be vigilant so that in the ultimate
eventuate there is no real failure of justice.
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 14 of 22

vii) The concept of liberal approach has to encapsule
the conception of reasonableness and it cannot be allowed
a totally unfettered free play.
viii) There is a distinction between inordinate delay and
a delay of short duration or few days, for to the former
doctrine of prejudice is attracted whereas to the latter it may
not be attracted. That apart, the first one warrants strict
approach whereas the second calls for a liberal delineation.
ix) The conduct, behaviour and attitude of a party relating to
its inaction or negligence are relevant factors to be taken into
consideration. It is so as the fundamental principle is that the
courts are required to weigh the scale of balance of justice
in respect of both parties and the said principle cannot be
given a total go by in the name of liberal approach.
x) If the explanation offered is concocted or the grounds
urged in the application are fanciful, the courts should be
vigilant not to expose the other side unnecessarily to face
such a litigation.
xi) It is to be borne in mind that no one gets away with fraud,
misrepresentation or interpolation by taking recourse to the
technicalities of law of limitation.
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 15 of 22

xii) The entire gamut of facts are to be carefully
scrutinized and the approach should be based on the
paradigm of judicial discretion which is founded on objective
reasoning and not on individual perception.
xiii) The State or a public body or an entity representing
a collective cause should be given some acceptable
latitude.”
25. Now, coming to the instant case. Vide the impugned order dated
25.11.2024, the Commission allowed the prayer of the appellants for
extension of time for commissioning of the power project up to 21.04.2025
but at the same time directed them to pay compensation to CTUIL as a
condition for retaining the connectivity granted to them at Bikaner-II. As
noted in the impugned order by the Commission, the appellant had given
an undertaking vide affidavit dated 28.10.2024 to the Commission that the
project would be commissioned before 24.04.2025. The appellants even
paid a sum of Rs.9.5 crores to CTUIL as compensation for the period
20.10.2024 to 21.04.2025 as per the impugned order of the Commission
between 06.12.2024 and 04.04.2025 notwithstanding the fact that they
had filed a review petition before the Commission on 02.01.2025 seeking
review of the impugned order. Such conduct of the appellants clearly
indicates their commitment to commission the project by 21.04.2025.
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 16 of 22

Despite the fact that the appellants were not satisfied with the impugned
order in so far as it directed to pay compensation to CTUIL for retaining
the connectivity, they appear to have paid the sum of Rs.9.5 Crores to the
CTUIL in order to avoid coercive action and to ensure that the work on the
project proceeds without any impediment. However, for certain reasons,
the appellants were not able to commission the project by 21.04.2025 and
accordingly, they approached the Commission by way of petition no.452
of 2025 seeking extension of further 65 days i.e. till 25.06.2025. During
the proceedings of this petition, the connectivity granted to the appellants
came to be revoked by CTUIL vide letter dated 23.04.2025, which was
subsequently put in abeyance by the Commission vide order dated
24.04.2025 passed in that petition.
26. It further appears that the full connectivity for the appellants power
project was being delayed even after the commissioning of the project on
25.06.2025 and accordingly, the appellants had to approach the Hon'ble
High Court of Delhi vide writ petition no.13641 of 2025 seeking direction
for expeditious operationalization of connectivity/GNA. Concededly, in
the status report dated 22.09.2025 filed by CTUIL and Power Grid Narela
Transmission Limited (PNTL) in the said writ petition, it was acknowledged
that Khetri-Narela line was incomplete and was likely to be commissioned
only by December, 2025. Even after the commissioning of the said Khetri-
Narela line on 10.12.2025, connectivity was not made effective for the
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 17 of 22

appellants power project by CTUIL even though the same was made
effective for all other projects connected to Bikaner-II. It is after the
passing of final order dated 12.12.2025 by the Commission in petition
no.452 of 2025 that the connectivity to the appellants power project was
restored fully by CTUIL at Bikaner-II and GNA was made effective for the
power project of the appellants from 14.12.2025 thereby permitting the
appellants to evacuate the entire 300MW power from the project.
27. The above noted sequence of events would manifestly demonstrate
that the appellants were making all out efforts to commission their power
project and to ensure seamless connectivity for it in order to evacuate the
power generated in the project despite facing various impediments for
which they had to file another petition before the Commission as well as
had to approach the Delhi High Court by way of a writ petition. It cannot
be said that all these proceedings were in no manner, connected to the
issues raised in the instant appeal i.e. extension of commissioning date of
the power project and the retention of the connectivity without payment of
any compensation.
28. Since, the appellants had paid a sum of Rs.9.5 cores to CTUIL as
compensation for the period 20.10.2024 to 21.04.2024 in terms of the
impugned order, they appear to have shifted focus to completion of the
power project and its commissioning within the extended time as allowed
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 18 of 22

by the Commission in the impugned order. Meanwhile, connectivity issue
came up as CTUIL firstly revoked the connectivity granted to the
appellants, on 23.04.2025 which was, however, kept in abeyance by the
Commission vide order dated 24.04.2025 passed in subsequent petition
no.452/2025 filed by the appellants. Even thereafter also the appellants
were allowed only partial connectivity and full connectivity was being
delayed on account of non-operationalization of Khetri-Narela
Transmission Line. Full connectivity came to be granted to the appellants
only on 14.12.2025 after passing of final order dated 12.12.2025 by the
Commission in petition no.452/2025. Evidently, the appellants were
embroiled in these issues and thought it prudent to wait for the outcome
of petition no.452/2025 before filing the instant appeal before this Tribunal.
We do not find any malafide or lack of due diligence in this regard on the
part of the appellants. The appellants were justified in delaying the filing
of the instant appeal till the power project was commissioned and full
connectivity was made available to the same. Assuming that the
appellants were unable to complete and commission the power project
within the extended time granted by the Commission or the petition
no.452/2025 was dismissed by the Commission thereby resulting in
revocation of connectivity to the appellants’ power project, in that case,
the appellants may not have been left with any cause or occasion for
assailing the impugned order before this Tribunal. It is only when the
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 19 of 22

appellants commissioned the power project and were also successful in
obtaining full connectivity for the same on 14.12.2025 that they turned
their attention to the impugned order and commenced steps for filing the
appeal against the same.
29. When we consider the delay in filing the instant appeal on the part
of the appellants in the light of above referred circumstances, we are
unable to impute any inaction or negligence or lack of bonafides to the
appellants. The entire gamut of facts and circumstances that took place
after the passing of impugned order by the Commission, when scrutinized
in the light of legal principles enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
above referred judgments, leads to the only conclusion that the delay in
filing of the appeal on the part of the appellants is not so inordinate or
contumacious or deliberate as to warrant dismissal of the application
under consideration.
30. Further, we may also note that the appellants had preferred a review
petition before the Commission on 02.01.2025 seeking review of the
impugned order, it cannot be said that the appellants did not take any
steps to assail the impugned order within the period of 45 days stipulated
under the Electricity Act, 2003 for filing appeal before this Tribunal.
Probably, the appellants realized that they may not succeed in the review
petition and accordingly withdrew the same on 03.03.2025. Normally, this
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 20 of 22

Tribunal, while computing the period of delay in filing the appeal, discounts
the time period spent by the appellant while pursuing the review petition
before the Commission. Therefore, if we take these 60 days, during which
period the review petition was pending disposal before the Commission,
out of consideration for computing the period of delay, the same is
reduced to 308 days only. We may also note that this Tribunal has been
liberal in condoning the delay of upto one year (365 days) in filing the
appeal, albeit, on payment of costs ranging from Rs.20,000/- to
Rs.2,00,000/- in order to do complete justice between the parties.
Reference, in this regard, is made by the learned counsel for the
appellants to order dated 30.01.2026 passed in DFR No.446/2025, order
dated 05.08.2025 passed in DFR No.164/2025, order dated 04.07.2025
passed in DFR No.137/2025, order dated 25.04.2025 passed in DFR
No.68/2025, order dated 06.01.2025 passed in DFR No.502/2024 etc.
31. Considering the above referred circumstances which, according to
the appellants were responsible for delay in filing the instant appeal, it is
difficult to accept the submissions of the learned counsel for the 2nd
respondent CTUIL that the delay was deliberate or there is been any lack
of bonafide on the part of the appellants. Adopting the liberal and
purposive interpretation of the term “sufficient cause” as advocated by the
Apex Court in Shivamma case, we are of the opinion that demands of
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.62 of 2028 in DFR 21 of 2026 Page 21 of 22

justice would be met in case the delay in filing the appeal is condoned
subject to payment of costs.
32. Therefore, the instant application is hereby allowed and the delay in
filing the appeal is condoned subject to the appellants paying costs of
Rs.1,50,000/- (Rupees one lakh and fifty thousand only) to 2nd respondent
CTUIL within four weeks from today and filing the proof of payment of
costs in the Registry of this Tribunal within two weeks thereafter.
Needless to add here that in case of failure to pay such costs within the
stipulated period or failure to file proof of payment of costs within the
stipulated period, the appeal shall stand dismissed as time barred.
DFR NO.21 OF 2026

The appellants shall file rejoinder, if any, within four weeks thereafter.
